title: What Houseplants Really Do to the Air Indoors
topic: home and living / indoor plants and air quality

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: A shelf of leafy plants is often sold as a way of cleaning the air at home, and the promise is a pleasant one: buy a fern, breathe better. Researchers who have tried to measure it have found something more complicated. Plants do change a room, but not always in the way the label on the pot suggests, and how much they change it depends on what is measured, on which plant does the work, and on how much fresh air the room already gets.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: The first study was run in three offices of a modern, well-insulated building in Canberra, Australia, by a team led by Junzhiwei Jiang. The rooms were chosen because they resembled one another closely: each had a ceiling 3.0 metres high, a window area of 4.3 square metres and the same northern outlook, so that daylight could not be blamed for whatever the plants appeared to do. Every office was measured three times over: empty, with five potted ferns, and with eighteen. The air conditioning was switched off throughout, because a running system shifts so much air that it would have buried any effect the plants had. Sensors sat 0.8 metres above the floor, roughly where a seated worker breathes.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Humidity was the one measure that clearly responded. With no plants, the median relative humidity was 29.1 per cent, dry enough to leave eyes and throats uncomfortable. Five ferns raised it to 38.9 per cent, and eighteen ferns to 49.2 per cent. The mechanism is ordinary: water drawn up through the roots evaporates from the leaves, so the more leaf surface a room holds, the more water vapour it gains. Damp air brings its own risks, but the readings never passed 70 per cent, the level at which mould becomes a concern.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The other two measures refused to move. Neither the air temperature nor the carbon dioxide concentration differed meaningfully between the bare offices and the crowded ones. Photosynthesis does take up carbon dioxide, but a person working in a small room releases it far faster than a few pots of leaves can absorb it, and in a building of this standard whatever they take up is quickly diluted by ventilation. Because the readings were collected only in daylight hours, when the plants were most active, the trial says nothing about the night.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The second study put the question the other way round. Instead of a room, Jing Chen and colleagues used a sealed box: a chamber one metre on every side, holding one plant at a time. Four-year-old saplings of five garden species, each grown in a 21-litre pot, were tested in turn, and particles were pumped through at three rates, giving concentrations of roughly 4,100, 3,000 and 800 per cubic centimetre. After a plant was sealed in, the team waited ten minutes before recording anything, so that the air inside had time to settle.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The species mattered more than expected. The Japanese pagoda tree collected the most, and the reason was visible under a microscope: its leaves carry deep grooves and fine hairs on both surfaces, and a rough surface holds particles that a smooth one lets pass. Japanese kerria, whose leaves were the smoothest and almost hairless, collected the least, and the pagoda tree's deposition rate was one and a half to two times higher. The Chinese honey locust, with thicker and waxier leaves, did its best work on the largest particles, removing 33.12 per cent of the coarse fraction. The purple-leaf peach has grooves but few hairs, yet it led on the smallest particles, taking out 39.86 per cent.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: To find out what had actually stuck, the leaves were rinsed in deionised water and shaken, because only material lifted off the surface could be measured. A pagoda tree leaf was carrying 5.286 micrograms of sulphate for every square centimetre; the same area of kerria leaf held 1.714 micrograms.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Then came the awkward part. When ordinary outdoor air was pumped through the same chambers instead of a prepared mist, the plants no longer reliably lowered anything. At eight in the morning the chamber holding the honey locust contained more particles than the empty control chamber, and at six in the evening the kerria chamber did the same. The likely reason is not that the leaves gave dust back, but that a bushy plant slows the air moving through a small space, so particles linger instead of passing through.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: A third team, led by Hiroyuki Fukumoto, changed the question from air to people. Eighteen office workers spent five minutes in each of three rooms, one planted in a Japanese style, one with tropical species and one bare, before sitting attention tests. The planted rooms did something to mood: the Japanese arrangement produced less negative feeling than the bare room, and less than the tropical arrangement, although neither lifted positive feeling. Performance was untouched, since accuracy and reaction times were the same in all three rooms.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: Put together, the three studies point to a modest conclusion. A generous number of plants will make a dry room noticeably less dry, and a well-chosen arrangement may make it feel calmer to sit in. Filtering, though, is the wrong word for what a shelf of pots does, because what a leaf catches in a sealed chamber is a poor guide to an occupied home, where opening a window still shifts more of everything than the plants ever will.
